The rapid evolution of the interstellar medium is driven by complex interactions between magnetic fields and plasma. To better understand these processes, researchers have used the imaging capabilities of the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) to study the behavior of the solar chromosphere. IRIS's ability to capture detailed images of the solar atmosphere has revealed the presence of transient brightenings in the Si IV emission line, which are associated with the occurrence of flares. These brightenings are often accompanied by changes in the spectral characteristics of the Si IV line, including shifts in its central wavelength and the appearance of broad wings. To better understand these changes, researchers have analyzed the Si IV spectra of a flare observed by IRIS at a sub-second cadence. They found that the Si IV line profile changes significantly during the flare, with the line becoming broader and shifting to longer wavelengths. These changes are consistent with the presence of non-thermal motions in the solar atmosphere, which are driven by the release of magnetic energy. The results of this study provide new insights into the behavior of the solar chromosphere during flares and highlight the importance of high-resolution spectroscopy in understanding the complex interactions between magnetic fields and plasma in the solar atmosphere.

The long-standing strong CP problem is a fundamental issue in particle physics, which our research aims to resolve by examining the implications of the Poincar\'e theorem on the EDM of the electron. By applying this theorem, we demonstrate that the CP-violating parameter $\bar{\theta}$ is not an arbitrary value but rather a fixed quantity, which in turn allows us to derive a new relationship between $\bar{\theta}$ and the axion mass. This novel connection provides a new perspective on the strong CP problem and may offer a potential solution to the hierarchy problem.

The primary goal of this research is to understand the underlying mechanisms that affect the critical angle for creating nanopatterns in materials that have been altered by radiation. To achieve this, the researchers used a computer simulation to model how individual atoms move and interact within a thin layer of a specific material, and how this movement affects the formation of nanopatterns. The results showed that the critical angle for creating these patterns is influenced by the way atoms move and interact within the material, and that this effect is more pronounced in areas where the material is less dense. The researchers also found that the way atoms move and interact within the material is influenced by the size and shape of the nanopatterns, and that the critical angle for creating these patterns is more sensitive to the size and shape of the nanopatterns in certain areas of the material.

The rapid expansion of the software industry has led to an increase in source code plagiarism cases, which has prompted the need for effective detection methods. This study presents a novel approach to identifying code plagiarism by converting source code into path graphs and comparing them using graph similarity metrics. The authors propose a C# implementation of this method, which has been tested on a diverse set of C# programs and evaluated against existing plagiarism detection tools. The results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is both efficient and accurate in detecting plagiarized code, and its performance surpasses that of traditional text-based methods.

This text explores the properties and characteristics of metric near subgroups, with a particular focus on free groups.

Log-concave density estimation is a widely used statistical method, but its application is often limited by the computational complexity of its likelihood function. The existing approaches, which involve solving a complex optimization problem, are impractical for large datasets. In response, we have developed a new method that transforms the likelihood maximization into a more tractable log-concave polytope volume problem. By employing a Monte Carlo approach, we have created an algorithm that efficiently approximates the optimal solution. The proposed method has several advantages, including its ability to handle large datasets and its capacity to incorporate prior knowledge. The results of our experiments demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency, and its application to real-world data has yielded promising outcomes.

We introduce a new entropic sampling technique that utilizes the Wang-Landau method to analyze granular packings in a two-dimensional vertical channel. This method enables the calculation of the logarithm of the density of states, which in turn allows us to determine the entropy and microstates of granular packings at any energy level. By using this technique, we have successfully reconstructed the pressure-volume isotherms of granular packings, which align with the predictions of the dry granular model. Additionally, we have analyzed the fluctuations in volume and pressure, which are consistent with the predictions of the model, and we have also investigated the microstates of granular packings at different volume levels. This technique provides valuable insights into the underlying physics of granular matter and its behavior under different conditions.

The Adventurer-Director Game is a two-player graph game, played by an adventurer and a director on a connected undirected graph. The adventurer aims to reach a designated destination vertex, while the director attempts to prevent this. The adventurer can move to any adjacent vertex, while the director can add an edge between vertices in each round, maintaining graph simplicity. The adventurer wins if they reach the destination, otherwise the director wins. We investigate the game's solvability and the director's optimal strategy, focusing on specific graph types including trees, unicyclic graphs, and complete bipartite graphs.

Our results are validated through numerical simulations of Gaussian processes, which exhibit both stationary and nonstationary behavior.

This is an ongoing effort, with various initiatives aiming to influence educational institutions and the general public. This paper outlines the Space Voyage project, a data science curriculum designed for elementary and middle school students. Space Village utilizes tangible data representations to facilitate hands-on learning and understanding. This research paper describes the Space Village approach and presents the initial findings from a classroom setting involving data bricks.

A significant amount of data is transmitted through Data-Flow Graphs (DAGs) in software-defined networking (SDN) data planes, which are crucial for the network's performance. However, not all DAGs are essential for the system's operation, as some are temporary and only exist during specific network events. This research focuses on identifying the DAGs that are vital for the system's functionality, as these are the ones that need to be preserved in case of network disruptions. We introduce a novel approach to identify these operational DAGs by analyzing the DAGs that have been observed in real-world SDN environments. This method allows us to identify DAGs that are crucial for the system's functionality, as they are the ones that are consistently present in real-world SDN environments. We have tested our approach on a large dataset of DAGs collected from a real-world SDN environment and found that it is effective in identifying operational DAGs. This research contributes to the field of SDN by providing a new approach to identify operational DAGs, which can be used to improve the resilience of SDN environments.

A significant challenge in disentangled representation learning lies in its reliance on strong assumptions about the underlying data-generating process, which can be difficult to verify. To address this, we explore the use of relational information to guide learning of disentangled representations, particularly in a setting where only limited data is available. Our approach leverages a separate relational dataset to learn relationships between object attributes, enabling the model to identify and isolate latent factors of variation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, which show that relational information can significantly enhance the disentanglement of representations and improve downstream task performance.

In the context of real-time lattice QCD, our research focuses on the application of Bayesian estimation methods to determine the expected behavior of QCD systems. By utilizing the principles of the Maximum Entropy principle, our approach is based on the assumption that the expected behavior of QCD systems is the most probable outcome given the available data. We have successfully applied this method to the pure gluon theory and obtained results that are consistent with analytical calculations. Furthermore, our approach is being extended to include quarks and gauge theories with matter, and we are exploring its potential to make predictions for the expected behavior of QCD systems in the presence of quarks.

In a hybrid system comprising a quantum dot and a superconducting island, we've observed charge-tunneling events between the two. By applying a voltage to the dot, we've seen that the interaction between the dot and the island is significantly influenced by the supercurrent. Our experiments show that the dot's charge state can be detected by measuring the superconducting island's response, which is a first demonstration of this phenomenon. Our results indicate that the dot's charge state can be transferred to the island, which is a crucial step in developing hybrid quantum systems.

The development of new drugs is a complex and resource-intensive process, often involving a significant amount of time and money. To address these challenges, researchers have been exploring the use of artificial intelligence to accelerate drug discovery. In this study, we present a novel generative model that can efficiently generate molecules with specific target properties, such as binding affinity to a particular protein. Our model, based on a combination of energy-driven generative models and graph neural networks, is able to learn from a large dataset of known drug structures and their properties, and then use this knowledge to generate new, effective drug candidates. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to a range of drug discovery tasks, including the generation of molecules with specific binding affinities to the protein p53. Our results show that our model is able to generate high-quality drug candidates that are comparable to or better than those generated by existing methods, and that can be used as a starting point for further drug development.

Interactive systems are becoming increasingly complex, and their behavior is difficult to model and understand. To address this challenge, we have developed a new approach called the Token-Guided Graph (TGG), which is a meta-model for describing interactive systems. Our method uses a unique representation that combines the principles of interaction devices and their behavior. By using a visual language based on graph rewriting, we can easily represent and analyze the behavior of interactive systems. Our method has been implemented in a tool that allows designers to explore and understand the behavior of their systems. Our approach has been tested on a variety of systems, and the results show that it is an effective method for modeling and understanding interactive systems.

To better understand the history of the LMC, researchers have analyzed the velocity field of the outer regions of the LMC, which has been found to be rotating in a way that is consistent with the SMC's influence. The widespread use of smart meters in modern power distribution networks has enabled utilities to collect granular data on energy consumption, leading to the development of various applications, such as demand forecasting and load profiling. However, this data collection is vulnerable to manipulation by smart meters, which can be exploited by energy thieves to conceal their true energy usage. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed several smart metering-based methods for detecting energy theft, with the majority focusing on supervised machine learning approaches. This paper presents a novel approach to smart metering-based energy theft detection, leveraging the deep recurrent power network (DRPN) model to analyze smart meter data and identify anomalies. The proposed method is evaluated using real-world data from the UK's smart meter rollout, and its performance is compared to existing methods, with the results indicating that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and robustness.

We develop a topological inductive method for creating all compact surface graphs, 
which are defined as connected graphs embedded topologically in compact surfaces.
This method enables the construction of all such surface graphs of any genus.
Key to this method is the concept of a surface graph's skeleton, 
which is a minor of the surface graph that captures its topological essence.
We demonstrate that every compact surface graph can be obtained from a planar graph 
through edge subdivisions and the addition of handles, which can be visualized as 
introducing cycles with two connecting edges.

Measurements of the lifetimes of specific baryons, namely $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$, have been conducted using data collected from proton-proton collisions at the LHCb experiment. These measurements were taken from a large dataset of 900 picobarns, which was obtained from collisions at a high energy level of 7 TeV. The lifetimes of these baryons were determined by analyzing their decay patterns and were found to be $0.181$ ps and $0.147$ ps for $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ respectively. These results are consistent with previous measurements and provide a more precise estimate of their lifetimes.

Hyperspectral image classification is a critical task in remote sensing, requiring efficient and accurate methods. Recent unsupervised approaches have shown promise, but they often struggle with the complexity of hyperspectral data. To address this, a novel framework called SCCSC is proposed, which combines subspace clustering and similarity constraints to improve classification performance. The framework uses a two-stage process, first identifying the most relevant spectral bands and then applying a similarity-constrained subspace clustering method to the selected bands. The results demonstrate that SCCSC outperforms existing methods, achieving superior classification accuracy and computational efficiency.

The uneven surface of Arctic sea ice, which influences heat transfer and the ice's growth, is influenced by the formation of a complex snow cover. To better understand this process, we developed a simplified model of how snow accumulates on Arctic sea ice, which takes into account the uneven distribution of the ice's surface. The model reveals that the topography of the ice beneath the snow plays a significant role in the formation of a rough snow cover, which is influenced by the interaction between the ice and the snow. The model also shows that the snow cover can be affected by the rate at which it melts and the amount of wind that blows across the ice, which can cause the snow to drift and accumulate in certain areas. The model provides a new perspective on the formation of a complex snow cover and highlights the importance of the ice's surface in shaping the snow's structure.

In this research, we investigate the dynamic quantum Zeno effect in interactions between cold atoms and molecules using a unique dynamic magnetic field approach. By applying this method, we reveal a distinct dynamic Zeno effect in cold atom-molecule scattering, which is characterized by a significant reduction in the rate of inelastic scattering when the switching frequency of the magnetic field is sufficiently high. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the dynamic Zeno effect in cold atom-molecule scattering is a result of the suppression of inelastic scattering events, and that the scattering rate can be precisely controlled by adjusting the magnetic field switching frequency. Our findings provide a new approach to studying the dynamic Zeno effect in cold atom-molecule scattering and may have potential applications in the development of novel quantum simulation and computation devices.

We have developed a broad approach to deriving the It\^o-Langevin equation from the Kramers equation, which results from a coarse-graining of the system's phase space. This approach reveals that the It^o-Langevin equation is a direct outcome of non-extensive statistical mechanics.

Weyl semimetal nodes, which are typically found in materials with broken time-reversal symmetry, can be created in optical lattices without this symmetry. We investigated a specific type of optical lattice, which is characterized by a unique symmetry, and discovered that it can host Weyl nodes with complex topological properties. By using numerical simulations, we found that this optical lattice can exhibit different types of topological phases, including a higher-order topological phase, which is unique to optical lattices. We also discovered that this optical lattice can be used to create a specific type of topological phase, which is characterized by a specific type of edge state. Furthermore, we found that this optical lattice can be used to create a specific type of topological phase, which is characterized by a specific type of edge state. This discovery has important implications for the study of topological phases in optical lattices.

A novel blockchain-based protocol has been developed to enable fair and efficient distributed computing. This decentralized protocol allows users to rent their computing resources and earn rewards from others, while ensuring fair resource allocation and reward distribution. The protocol's security is guaranteed through a novel proof-of-work mechanism, which prevents malicious users from exploiting the system. The protocol's efficiency is further enhanced by a fair task distribution algorithm that minimizes the impact of user behavior on resource allocation. The protocol's fairness is also ensured by a reward distribution algorithm that prevents users from withholding their resources. The protocol's efficiency and fairness are demonstrated through simulations, which show that it can achieve high levels of fairness and efficiency.

A novel framework for reduced reference point cloud perceptual quality assessment is introduced, incorporating an objective quality metric. This approach involves a reference model for comparison, allowing for a more efficient quality evaluation process. The proposed metric is applied to 3D point cloud compression systems, facilitating the development of a rate control method. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed metric in accurately predicting perceptual quality and enabling the optimization of coding parameters.

We investigate the relationship between the boundary theory of strongly coupled plasma and its planar AdS dual, focusing on the phase transition between the plasma and its quark-gluon plasma state. We propose a phase diagram for the strongly coupled plasma, derived from the holographic model, and examine the phase transition's order parameter, which is the plasma's energy density. We then discuss the AdS/CFT correspondence and its implications for the plasma's properties.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to a surge in interest in self-supervised learning (SSL) for medical imaging, particularly in pre-training models on vast unlabeled datasets. This study introduces a novel, slice-based SSL approach for the classification of anomalies in MRI images. The proposed method leverages the transformer architecture to capture long-range dependencies within individual image slices, and employs a multi-task SSL framework to enhance the pre-trained model's representation. The model is then fine-tuned on a labeled dataset for knee X-ray classification. Our approach surpasses state-of-the-art models, achieving a notable 1.5% boost in AUC over the baseline, and outperforms other SSL methods by a 0.8% margin in AUC.

The rapid evolution of typefaces has led to a vast array of options, but the process of creating new styles is often labor-intensive and requires specialized expertise. To address this challenge, we've developed a new approach that enables the creation of new typefaces from a single example in a few seconds. Our method, based on a novel framework called StyleGAN-Editor, combines the strengths of two existing techniques: style-based and content-based editing. By integrating these methods, we've created a system that can effectively transfer the style of one character to another, even when they're not similar. Our approach involves a two-stage process: first, we use a style encoder to capture the unique features of the input character, and then we use a style editor to apply this style to other text. Our results show that this method can generate high-quality style transfers between diverse alphabets and languages, and it can also be used to generate new typefaces from a single example.

We examine the properties of a chiral fluid under the influence of a twist in the spatial dimensions. This twist is equivalent to a magnetic field in terms of its impact on the fluid's behavior. This research builds upon the thermal equilibrium conditions of the Chiral Magnetic Effect and the Chiral vortical effect. This investigation is conducted using the framework of hydrodynamics and a perturbative approach to the underlying quantum field theory. This research is particularly relevant to the properties of quark-gluon plasma, which exhibits chirality due to the presence of light quarks.

A key challenge in adaptive video streaming is striking a balance between video quality and network congestion. To address this issue, a novel QoE optimization framework is proposed, which is grounded in a user-specific model of video streaming. This model is based on a digital representation of the user's device, which captures the impact of various factors, including user preferences, on the user's experience. By leveraging this model, a real-time optimization algorithm is developed to adjust the video streaming parameters, thereby maximizing the user's experience. The proposed framework is evaluated through simulations, which demonstrate its ability to enhance QoE compared to standard video streaming protocols.

The KM3NeT/ARCA, a high-energy neutrino telescope, is being constructed in the Mediterranean Sea and will utilize the Cherenkov radiation produced by charged particles to identify the direction and energy of the neutrinos. The telescope's ability to differentiate between single and double water cascades is crucial for minimizing background interference from muons. A new method for identifying double waterfall events has been developed, utilizing the time and amplitude of the signals collected by the telescope's sensors. The proposed algorithm was tested using simulated data and demonstrated a high accuracy rate of 90% in identifying double waterfall events, while achieving a background rejection rate of 99.999% for single waterfall muon events.

This paper delves into the conditions for the accuracy of a periodic nonlinear Schrödinger equation with stochastic noise in dispersion modeling. By establishing a framework for analyzing the equation's stochastic behavior, we derive the conditions under which solutions are stable and accurate. Our approach relies on the properties of a specific type of stochastic process, which allows us to study the equation's long-term behavior. We then establish a link between this process and the equation's accuracy, using it to prove that solutions are stable and accurate. Finally, we apply our results to two specific cases, demonstrating the method's effectiveness in deriving accurate solutions for these equations.

This study investigates the optimal allocation of data streams across multiple wireless channels to minimize packet transmission delays, while ensuring reliable data delivery. The problem is complex due to the interplay between data stream distribution and channel coding, as well as the need to account for the packetization of these streams. To address this challenge, we develop a new method that combines data stream allocation with channel coding, taking into consideration the packet delay constraints. The proposed approach is evaluated using a mathematical model that considers the packetization of data streams and the delay constraints. The results show that this method outperforms traditional methods that separate data stream allocation and channel coding, as well as the packet size optimization method.

The Sgr A East nebula, a prominent structure in the vicinity of the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way, is a key area for understanding the evolution of the galaxy. A supernova explosion approximately 2 million years ago is believed to have triggered the Sgr A East nebula, but the exact location of the supernova remains uncertain. To investigate this issue, we have conducted a detailed analysis of the supernova's origin, utilizing data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the Spitzer Space Telescope. Our findings indicate that the supernova likely occurred in a region near the center of the galaxy, where it would have been able to produce the Sgr A East nebula as observed today. This analysis has significant implications for our understanding of the galaxy's evolution and the formation of its central supermassive black hole.

Recent experimental findings on B-meson decays have sparked interest in lepton flavor universality violation, with the theoretical basis of the Standard Model providing a clear framework for comparison. This article examines the Standard Model's origin and magnitude of LFU violations in B decays, as well as potential Beyond the Standard Model explanations. It also offers an outlook on future experimental discoveries that could provide definitive answers regarding the Standard Model's validity.

Our system, developed for the DISRPT2021 Shared Task, focuses on automating discourse analysis by identifying, labeling, and organizing segments of meaning in texts, as well as detecting and categorizing connective words. The system, built using a combination of transformer-based models and a rule-based system, achieved notable success in the track-specific track, securing first place with an impressive F1 score of 80.3%, and demonstrated strong performance in the main track, securing fifth place with an F1 score of 75.3%.

The upcoming 6G networks are expected to revolutionize the Internet of Things, enabling a wide range of applications such as self-driving vehicles, remote surgery, and smart homes. However, the massive data generated by these applications poses a significant challenge for the 6G networks, necessitating the use of distributed computing to alleviate the burden. This has led to the emergence of a new paradigm in distributed computing, known as clear computing, which aims to enhance the efficiency of distributed computing by optimizing the use of available resources. This paper presents a novel blockchain-based solution, known as BEAT, which aims to address the key challenges in clear computing, including resource allocation, data security, and accountability. BEAT is designed to provide a secure and trustworthy framework for clear computing, ensuring that the data generated by the 6G networks is protected and that the users are accountable for their actions.

The Okubo-Weiss criterion is a widely recognized indicator of vorticity stretching in two-dimensional flows. This study aims to explore the applicability of this criterion in fluid dynamics and magnetofluid systems. We begin by examining the criterion's effectiveness in two-dimensional incompressible flows, where it accurately predicts vortex formation. Next, we investigate its application in magnetofluid systems, where the criterion's accuracy is influenced by the relative strengths of vorticity and magnetic field gradients. We find that the criterion's effectiveness diminishes in magnetofluid systems, primarily due to the presence of magnetic field gradients. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that the criterion can still be useful in identifying regions of vorticity stretching in magnetofluid systems, provided that the vorticity gradients are significantly stronger than magnetic field gradients.

Lee-Wick theories are a type of non-local field theory that can be used to create a self-regulating model of the universe. This model is based on the idea that the universe's thermal evolution can be described by a modified version of the Boltzmann equation. By incorporating the effects of Lee-Wick particles, the model predicts that the universe's temperature will decrease over time, leading to a natural end to the inflationary period. This model also provides a potential explanation for the observed properties of dark matter and its relationship to the universe's thermal history.

We introduce StyTr$^2$, a transformer-based architecture that translates images into their styled counterparts. StyTr$^2$ is a transformer-based model that utilizes the attention mechanism to capture long-range dependencies in images. It consists of two main components: the encoder that extracts image features and the decoder that reconstructs the original image. To capture the style of the target image, StyTr$^2$ incorporates the style encoder that extracts the target style features and fuses them with the encoded image features. We evaluate StyTr$2$ on three datasets and demonstrate its superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of preserving the original image content and generating high-quality styled images. The code and pre-trained models of StyTr$^2$ are publicly available at https://github.com/ChaoYongLi/StyTr2.

The study of thermodynamic processes is facilitated by the concept of thermodynamic length, which quantifies the distance between equilibrium states in a thermodynamic system. Thermodynamic length is closely related to the dissipation of heat, and it has been suggested that it plays a significant role in the study of information processing. In this research, we demonstrate that the process of Landauer erasure can be optimized by maximizing the thermodynamic length, which results in a constant dissipation rate. This finding is supported by experimental results obtained from a colloidal particle in a trap.

We have conducted an in-depth analysis of the vector-like T quark's production and decay at future high-energy electron-positron colliders. Our study focused on the performance of these facilities, specifically the CEPC and ILC, in detecting the vector-like T quark. We investigated the cross-sections of the T quark's production channels, including single and pair production, and its decays into a single t quark and a light quark, as well as the Standard Model's t quark decaying into a b quark and a W boson. Our results indicate that, with a high luminosity of 10^36 cm^-2 s^-1, the ILC has the potential to discover a vector-like T quark with a mass of up to 1.2 TeV at a 5σ significance level. On the other hand, the CEPC's sensitivity to the vector-like T quark is lower due to its lower energy, but it can still detect T quarks with masses up to 800 GeV at a 5σ significance level.

The behavior of acoustic waves in nonhomogeneous fluids is analyzed using the principles of the Navier-Stokes equations, which reveal that the fluid's stability is contingent on its density gradient. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the fluid remains stable when the density gradient is positive and unstable when it is negative. Furthermore, it is shown that the presence of viscosity does not alter this fundamental stability criterion.

This article presents a weighted shift's characterization using spectral theory in the context of generalized directed semi-trees. It also establishes the analytic framework for weighted shifts in the specific generalization of directed semi-trees known as rooted trees.

The interaction between an extremely short, high-energy $\gamma$-ray pulse and a heavy metal target is investigated, considering the impact of the $\gamma$-ray pulse on the target in a state where the wavelength is equal to the distance between the target's atoms. The study focuses on the production of high-energy electron-electron-positron pairs and radioactive nuclei, particularly through the interaction between the $\gamma$-ray pulse and the target in a state where the wavelength is equal to the distance between the target's atoms. The study reveals that the production of high-energy electron-electron-positron pairs is significantly enhanced by the presence of the target in a state where the wavelength is equal to the distance between the target's atoms, and that the production of radioactive nuclei is significantly enhanced by the presence of the target in a state where the wavelength is equal to the distance between the target's atoms. The study also explores the potential applications of this phenomenon in the production of radioactive isotopes for medical and industrial applications.

This study introduces Event Recognition, a task that involves identifying and categorizing events within images, which is crucial for applications like traffic monitoring and surveillance. We propose a new approach to this task, which involves using graph convolutional neural networks to analyze event images. Our method leverages the diversity of image features and the importance of syntactic features to improve classification accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on established benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results.

This research investigates the theoretical foundations of Bayesian error-in-variable regression, focusing on sampling methods. Building on the work of B. Efron, we explore the geometric ergodicity of Gibbs and Metropolis sampling techniques for Bayesian error-in-variable models with a fixed prior distribution on regression coefficients. The results demonstrate that Gibbs sampling methods are universally applicable in Bayesian error-in-variable models, whereas geometric ergodicity in Metropolis sampling methods is contingent upon the prior distribution's tail behavior.

The ability to measure the environment's properties with high precision is crucial for the development of quantum technologies. Our research focuses on the application of quantum sensing to the measurement of magnetic fields. We have developed a novel approach to optimize the performance of quantum sensors by controlling the interaction between multiple qubits. Our method is based on the use of Hamiltonian simulation and the creation of entangled states, which enables the detection of magnetic fields with high sensitivity. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to the control of the spin-1/2 Ising model, which models the interaction between qubits. Our results show that the performance of our quantum sensor is limited by the presence of noise, but we have developed a robust control strategy that can improve its performance by a factor of 10. Our approach has the potential to be applied to the control of other quantum systems, such as quantum dots and superconducting qubits.

This research introduces a novel numerical method for analyzing nonlinear dynamical systems with random noise. The proposed approach is founded on the Krylov subspace technique, which is commonly employed to solve complex systems of linear equations. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated by its ability to provide accurate and efficient solutions for nonlinear dynamical systems, even in cases where the system's equations are difficult to solve analytically. The proposed method is shown to be particularly well-suited for systems with multiple variables and complex interactions, and its performance is evaluated through numerical experiments on a variety of benchmark problems. The results of these experiments demonstrate that the proposed method is capable of achieving high accuracy and efficiency, and its performance is comparable to that of other state-of-the-art methods for solving nonlinear dynamical systems.

We've developed a set of theoretical models to study how light interacts with complex media containing particles that absorb light in a nonlinear manner. These models, specifically the Monte Carlo simulation and the diffusion approximation, are used to predict how light behaves as it scatters through these media. Our research reveals that the behavior of light in these media is significantly influenced by the initial intensity of the light, leading to a decrease in the penetration depth of the light. This effect is particularly pronounced in media with low scattering rates, where the initial attenuation of the light is more significant. Our results also show that the diffusion approximation is effective in describing the behavior of light in these media, especially when the initial attenuation is taken into account.

Reinforcement learning has become a prominent area of research in artificial intelligence, with its applications extending to various domains such as robotics, gaming, and healthcare. However, the inherent complexity of RL algorithms often hinders their adoption due to a lack of transparency and interpretability. This challenge is particularly pressing in high-stakes fields where understanding the decision-making process is crucial. This study provides a comprehensive review of the current state of affairs in interpretable reinforcement learning, examining the existing methods and their limitations. We delve into the key components of this field, including the definition of interpretability, the evaluation of RL models, and the specific challenges associated with RL algorithms. Furthermore, the survey highlights the existing gaps in this area and proposes potential directions for future research.

This paper establishes a comprehensive framework for multi-valued logic systems that utilize a single variable, where the underlying values are drawn from a complete and finite lattice structure. The proposed system is characterized by its reliance on a unique, invariant semantics, thereby eliminating the need for additional constraints. The paper further explores the relationship between the system's semantic and syntactic properties, including a theorem that outlines the conditions under which the system's semantic and syntactic properties are equivalent. Notably, the system's semantic properties are characterized by a lattice-theoretic property known as the Dedekind-MacNeille completion.

This study investigates the Wiener chaos decomposition of the signature of a Gaussian process, focusing on a generalized version of the Brownian motion driven by a geometrically irreducible Gaussian process. We establish that the decomposition can be represented as an infinite sum of symmetric tensor fields, where each component corresponds to an order of the Gaussian process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this representation is unique and can be derived from the covariance kernel of the Gaussian process. We also derive an expression for the Lipschitz constant of the Gaussian process and show that the decomposition converges in the space of symmetric tensor fields. Additionally, we derive a formula for the variance of the Gaussian process, which is expressed in terms of the eigenvalues of the covariance kernel. Finally, we provide an example of a Gaussian process that satisfies the conditions of our main results, which is the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process.

In millimeter-wave cellular networks, the unique propagation characteristics enable a wide range of frequencies, which are subject to rapid variations in signal strength. This paper develops a statistical model to describe the performance of localization systems, taking into account the effects of signal fading and interference. By applying the derived model to a real-world scenario, we demonstrate its ability to accurately predict the performance of localization systems, which can be used to inform the design of network parameters.

We numerically demonstrate the phase transition in the Gross-Pitaevskii equation for a non-rotating Bose gas, utilizing the relative particle density in momentum space to distinguish between the normal and superfluid states. This approach is validated by comparing its results to known phase diagrams in momentum space. Our research also explores the dynamics of the order parameter, specifically the relative particle density, in both momentum and real space, and we find that it exhibits a discontinuity at the critical point in the normal to superfluid transition, and that it displays a sharp peak in momentum space for a system in the superfluid regime.

Recent advancements in image inpainting have been made using deep learning techniques, but current methods still struggle with preserving fine details and textures in the reconstructed image. To address this issue, we propose a novel two-tier inpainting approach that combines a deep encoder-decoder network with a detailed texture refinement module. The proposed method first fills in missing image areas using a deep neural network, and then refines the result with a texture refinement module that focuses on high-frequency details. To further enhance the quality of reconstructed images, we incorporate a self-supervised learning mechanism that enables the network to learn from its own output. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art image inpainting techniques in terms of both visual quality and objective evaluation metrics.

The Structured Thresholding Bandit problem is a complex extension of the multi-armed bandit issue, where the goal is to identify the optimal arm from a set of options, each possessing unique characteristics. In this scenario, the arms are arranged in a specific order, and the optimal solution involves finding a point where the mean reward exceeds a certain threshold. This research focuses on understanding the optimal arm's structure and the associated challenges in identifying it. A novel algorithm called Structured-UCB is developed, which adapts the widely used Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) method and achieves optimal results in terms of both sample complexity and convergence rates. Furthermore, the algorithm's performance is evaluated in a real-world application, demonstrating its effectiveness in a practical setting.

Our research builds on a series of papers that established a novel connection between P and NP through proof compression. We initially demonstrated that if PSPACE problems can be succinctly verified, then the ability to compress proofs within polynomial time would imply P = NP. This connection was further solidified by a separate study, which showed that if PSPACE problems can be succinctly verified, then the compressibility of proofs is equivalent to P = NP. This paper serves as an extension to these findings, which were initially presented in a separate, initially unpublished work.

The $H^\alpha$-flow is a geometric evolution process that deforms hypersurfaces in space, driven by their mean curvature. This flow is designed to maintain the concavity of hypersurfaces in space, particularly those with mean curvature. In this research, we prove that complete mean concave hypersurfaces, represented as graphs, will evolve under the $H^\alpha$-flow for a certain duration. This research also extends a well-known theorem by Peres and Soto, originally applicable to convex surfaces, to the broader category of mean concave hypersurfaces.

The fluctuations of vortex dipoles in a two-dimensional superfluid are analyzed through the lens of Coulomb gas sum laws. This study involves the derivation of these sum laws using two distinct methods: the vortex-vortex scattering amplitude and the vortex-antivortex pair creation amplitude. The Coulomb gas model is then mapped onto a complex $\phi^3$ theory, enabling the derivation of the structure factor and the distribution of vortex dipoles in terms of the coupling constant. The results are compared to a vortex-antivortex model, revealing the emergence of a vortex-antivortex bound state. The study also examines the effect of a repulsive interaction between vortex dipoles and the resulting implications for the structure factor and the distribution of vortex dipoles.

The widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in daily life has sparked a multitude of concerns and hopes, prompting a comprehensive examination of public opinion on the subject. This study delves into the attitudes of people from eight countries, including the US, UK, Germany, and others, to understand their perspectives on AI. Drawing from a survey of over 10,000 participants, our analysis reveals that the majority of individuals hold both apprehensions and aspirations regarding AI, with the most common concerns revolving around job displacement and the most common aspirations centered around the potential for AI to enhance human capabilities. Notably, our findings indicate that demographic factors such as age, gender, and education level significantly influence these perceptions.

The $\Xi_c^0$ to $\pi^-\Lambda_c^+$ decay is a highly suppressed process that is expected to be a key indicator of the Standard Model's third generation quark interactions. This study reports the first measurement of the branching ratio for this rare decay, utilizing a sample of 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected by the LHCb experiment at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The branching ratio is determined to be $(1.89 \pm 0.32 \pm 0.18 \pm 0.04) \times 10^{-4}$, where the uncertainties are statistical, systematic, and related to the $\Xi_c^0$ to $K^-\Lambda$ decay branching ratio. The study also examines the production cross-section of the $\Xi_c^0$ baryon and its polarization, as well as the mass difference between the $\Xi_c^0$ baryon and its decay product $\pi^-$.

This research aims to identify the fixed point of the product of two operators within Banach algebras. Initially, we establish that if the product of two operators is an approximate fixed point, then, under certain conditions, the product of the limits of these operators is equal to the limit of their product. Following this fundamental result, we apply it to various functional equations to demonstrate its utility.

Reinforcement learning algorithms, specifically Actor-Critic methods, have been highly successful in solving complex sequential decision-making problems. However, their performance is often hindered by the issue of high variance in the gradient estimates. To address this challenge, we introduce an innovative method that integrates the principles of geometric integration, specifically the symplectic integration of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, into Actor-Critic algorithms. By doing so, we significantly enhance the stability of the gradient updates and improve the overall performance of the learning process. Our proposed method is demonstrated through its successful application in a range of benchmark tasks, including the Acrobot, HalfCheetah, Hopper, and Walker2d, where it consistently outperforms the standard Actor-Critic algorithm.

We investigate the quantum phase diagram of a three-mode system with unequal coupling strengths to bosons, leading to distinct phases with unique properties. The presence of chiral quantum phases is a key feature, which arises from the imbalance in coupling strengths. The phase diagram is characterized by multiple transition lines, including two first-order lines and one second-order line, which meet at critical points. The critical points are further defined by the presence of two tricritical points, which mark the transition between first-order and second-order transitions. The critical behavior of the system is governed by the universality class of the 3D-Ising model. The study also reveals the existence of quantum critical points and their associated critical exponents, which are essential for understanding the system's behavior.

In multi-agent reinforcement learning, the credit assignment problem is a significant challenge. This study introduces a collaborative multi-agent learning framework that combines transfer learning and credit assignment techniques to enhance the efficiency of multi-agent systems. A novel method, called Level-Adaptive Credit Assignment, is proposed to facilitate the sharing of knowledge between agents at different levels of expertise. This approach enables the transfer of knowledge from advanced to less experienced agents, thereby accelerating the learning process. The effectiveness of this framework is demonstrated through simulations on the StarCraft II multi-agent learning benchmark.

This paper introduces a novel deep reinforcement learning framework for particle robots, which enables them to navigate and manipulate objects in a manner similar to biological systems. The proposed framework, which is based on a particle filter, allows for the representation of a robot's state as a distribution of particles, which can be updated using a combination of importance sampling and resampling. The effectiveness of this framework is demonstrated through simulations that involve navigating through complex environments and manipulating objects, which are modeled as a series of tasks with associated rewards. The results of these simulations show that the proposed framework is capable of learning effective policies for navigating and manipulating objects, which are robust to noise and uncertainty in the environment.

The detection of atomic species in the atmospheres of hot Jupiters has been a significant focus of research, with notable success in identifying certain elements such as H2O, CO, HCO+, and H2CO. However, K i has not been detected yet, despite being a common element in these planets. The detection of K i in the atmosphere of WASP-31b was attempted using the Keck/OSIRIS and VLT/UVES spectrographs, but no evidence was found. The analysis of the data was complicated by the presence of telluric features, which were removed using a novel method called ACCESS, which also provided a way to assess the accuracy of the results. The ACCESS method was found to be effective in removing telluric features and retrieving the true spectrum of the target star. The analysis of the data from the WASP-31 b transits revealed that the K i feature was not detected, with a 3σ upper limit of 0.14 ppm. The analysis also considered the possibility of clouds in the atmosphere of WASP-31b, which could explain the absence of the K i detection.

High-performance computing applications are increasingly being deployed in cloud environments, but the current infrastructure lacks a critical component - high-speed, non-volatile memory. This research aims to bridge this gap by evaluating the potential of high-speed, non-volatile memory in cloud-based HPC services. We examine the potential applications of this technology in cloud-based HPC services, including data-intensive tasks like machine learning and data analytics, as well as computational tasks like weather forecasting and fluid dynamics simulations. We also discuss the challenges associated with integrating this technology into cloud-based HPC services, including the need for new programming models and software tools, and the potential limitations of current technology. Finally, we outline our vision for cloud-based HPC services that leverage high-speed, non-volatile memory and outline the necessary steps to achieve this vision.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data analysis has become a crucial component of brain research, particularly in identifying patterns associated with various neurological conditions. However, accurately classifying fMRI data remains a significant challenge due to the vast amount of data and the inherent noise. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach that utilizes a contrastive learning framework to enhance fMRI data classification. Our method involves constructing a graph-based representation of fMRI data, which captures the functional connections between different brain regions. We then employ a contrastive graph learning model to extract meaningful features from the graph, which are subsequently used for accurate classification. Our experiments on a widely used fMRI dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding superior classification performance compared to existing methods.

Our research explores the algebraic and topological properties of Latin squares, specifically focusing on their symbol and entry totals. We examine the properties of $\mathbb{Z}_n$-multiplication tables and investigate the conditions under which their sums form a group. We also present a comprehensive analysis of the properties of cyclic and non-cyclic multiplication tables, including their sums and $\mathbb{Z}_n$-Gauss problems. Additionally, we demonstrate the connection between multiplication tables and the properties of finite fields, and we provide a detailed investigation of the Gauss problems associated with these tables.

When high-energy electrons traverse thin foils, they emit soft X-rays, which can be amplified into hard X-rays through the process of soft X-ray Cherenkov radiation. This process, which is triggered by the interaction of electrons with the atomic shells of the foils, has been investigated using 100 MeV electrons in foils made of beryllium and silicon. The study involved measuring the emitted X-rays using a specialized detector and comparing the results to theoretical predictions. The findings suggest that the emitted X-rays are primarily in the 1-10 keV range, which is consistent with the expected K-shell energies of the foils' constituent elements. The study also indicates that the emitted X-rays are predominantly emitted in the forward direction, which is consistent with the expected behavior of soft X-ray Cherenkov radiation.

The Universal Compositional Approach to semantics, UCCA, is a recent and innovative method for representing linguistic meaning that has garnered significant attention in the natural language processing field. A key aspect of UCCA is its reliance on identifying implicit arguments within sentences, which are often omitted from standard analysis. A recent UCCA-based dataset, TUCCA, was created to facilitate research in UCCA and its applications, particularly in the realm of natural language processing. A new, advanced UCCA dataset, UCCA+TUCCA, has been developed by combining existing UCCA annotations with machine learning-based implicit argument predictions. A comprehensive evaluation of the new dataset has been conducted, demonstrating its potential to enhance the performance of semantic parsing models.

Chest X-rays are frequently used to diagnose various respiratory conditions, but accurately pinpointing the affected areas is a labor-intensive task.  To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed a method that can automatically identify abnormal areas in chest X-rays without requiring detailed annotations.  This approach uses a technique called Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) to identify the regions in the X-ray images that are most likely to contain signs of disease.  By analyzing patterns in the data, the method can identify areas that are likely to be affected by the disease and use this information to train a model to identify abnormal areas in new X-ray images.  To improve the performance of the model, the researchers incorporated a technique called Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) and a method called Self-Directed Multiple Instance Learning (SDMIL) that allows the model to identify abnormal areas in the X-ray images without requiring detailed annotations.  The results of the study show that the proposed method outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, and can be used to diagnose various respiratory conditions with high accuracy.

In the context of model selection, we investigate a penalized version of the minimum Hellinger estimator, particularly when dealing with models that are not statistically equivalent. The method of determining optimal penalty values involves minimizing the worst-case loss across a range of scenarios. The proposed approach is applicable to small sample sizes and does not rely on asymptotic properties. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through a simulation study, which compares the small-sample performance of the penalized minimum Hellinger estimator to that of maximum likelihood estimation.

Our research focuses on binary sequences containing specific patterns, specifically the Prouit-Thue-Morse sequence, which is known for its intricate binary structure. We aim to identify and analyze recurring binary sequences within this complex sequence, which we refer to as binary motifs. By employing a systematic approach, we have successfully established a recursive method for calculating the number of unique binary motifs found in the Prouit-Thue-Morse sequence up to a certain length. Furthermore, our study reveals that the number of these motifs grows exponentially, with a particular growth rate that we have mathematically proven. We have also explored and derived a formula for the number of unique binary motifs within the Prouit-Thue-Morse sequence, which is a valuable piece of information for further analysis.

The performance of ensemble classifiers can be significantly improved by identifying the most suitable base classifiers for each instance through dynamic classifier selection. However, traditional DCS methods often overlook the fact that base classifiers within an ensemble tend to share similar performance. To address this, we developed a Hierarchical Dynamic Classifier Selection (HD-CS) method that leverages the performance of local subsets of base classifiers to identify the most suitable subset for each instance. By utilizing a hierarchical structure, HD-CS can reduce the number of classifiers required for classification, thereby minimizing the classification cost. Furthermore, we introduced a cost-sensitive version of HD-CS, known as Cost-Sensitive HD-CS, which takes into account the cost of base classifiers and the instances to further optimize classification efficiency. Experimental results on 11 benchmark datasets demonstrate that HD-CS outperforms existing DCS methods, and Cost-Sensitive HD-CS achieves comparable performance with reduced computational cost.

The Tianlai project is an ambitious radio telescope array located in China, designed to study the early universe through the lens of radio astronomy. Comprising a network of 1000+ radio antennas, the Tianlai experiment is set to explore the cosmic dawn and reionization periods, ultimately contributing to our understanding of the universe's evolution. As part of this endeavor, the Tianlai experiment will also be a valuable resource for studying the solar system and other celestial bodies. To support this ambitious project, the Tianlai team has developed an advanced data management pipeline, which integrates cutting-edge technologies to process and store vast amounts of data efficiently. This pipeline incorporates the use of the Apache Kafka system for real-time data streaming, the Apache Flink framework for data processing, and the Apache Parquet file format for efficient data storage. Furthermore, the Tianlai team has implemented a sophisticated data quality control system to ensure data integrity and reliability. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the Tianlai data management pipeline, highlighting its key features and capabilities.

First, we have successfully synthesized and studied the NbSi2N4, VSi2N4, and VSi2P4 monolayers using a scanning tunneling microscope. These monolayers exhibit distinct electronic properties, with NbSi2N4 and VSi2N4 showing metallic behavior, while VSi2P4 demonstrates semiconducting behavior. Notably, the VSi2N4 monolayer displays ferromagnetic properties, with a magnetic moment of 1.0 muB per unit cell, as confirmed by spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy. Furthermore, the magnetic properties of NbSi2N4 monolayer can be tuned by introducing defects, with a magnetic moment of 1.0 muB per defect. These findings pave the way for the creation of novel two-dimensional magnetic materials with tailored properties.

We introduce a novel method for generating positive definite functions on metric spaces, which generalizes techniques previously used to create pseudo-random fields. This approach is rooted in R. Gneiting's spatial covariance model and its extensions.

A semigroup is considered atomic if every element can be broken down into a sequence of atoms, where an atom cannot be expressed as the product of two non-unit elements within the semigroup. This paper explores atomicity in the context of cancellative semigroups with a positive order, focusing on the conditions that make it 'atomic' or even 'strongly atomic,' where each element is a product of atoms. We establish that this property is indeed achievable in such semigroups, and we further prove that this property is indeed achievable in any ordered group, provided the order is positive.

The case-case method is a widely used approach to estimate the attributable fraction among the exposed in observational studies. This technique relies on the assumption that the distribution of the exposure in the total population is identical to the distribution in the control group. However, when the control group is chosen from the total population, this assumption may not hold, leading to biased estimates of the attributable fraction. To address this issue, we developed a new method that utilizes case description data to adjust for the bias in the control group's exposure distribution. This method is applicable to both binary and continuous confounders and can be used in various settings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a simulation study and illustrate its practical application with an example from a study examining the association between obesity and cardiovascular disease.

We establish a cohomological reciprocity law that encompasses both Bloch's formula for Chow groups of zero-cycles and a theorem related to the weak Abel map for curves, and this law is shown to have applications in proving the existence of rational points on the product of an abelian variety and a smooth curve over a regular field.

Measurements of the production cross-section ratio for the $\Upsilon$(1S), $\Upsilon$(2S), and $\Upsilon$(3S) states in proton-proton collisions at 7 TeV are presented. Data were collected using the CMS detector at the LHC, with an integrated cross-section of 1.0 inverse nanobarns. A method of calculating the ratio from the ratio of the yields of the states in the muon pair decay channel, adjusted for the branching fractions and efficiency, is used. A study of the dependence of the ratio on the transverse momentum of the states and the number of charged particles in the event is also conducted. Results show that the ratio is relatively constant with transverse momentum, with a value of approximately 0.075. A significant correlation between the ratio and the number of charged particles in the event is observed, with a value of approximately 0.002 per charged particle.

We investigate the thermodynamic properties of a strongly coupled quantum dot connected to two quantum wires, employing the replica trick to calculate the free energy and entropy of the system. By considering a quantum dot with a strong Coulomb interaction, we derive an approximate solution to the Kondo model, which is then compared to the results obtained from the numerical renormalization group method.

This article establishes a broader application of the Geometric Modulus Principle, initially developed for real analytic functions, and demonstrates its relevance to holomorphic and harmonic functions. The findings are then applied to determine the growth rate of the Geometric Modulus for holomorphic and harmonic functions within specific domains.

The discrete nonpolynomial Schrodinger equation, which models the dynamics of cold-atom Bose-Einstein condensates, is studied in the context of a one-dimensional lattice with dipole-dipole interactions. We investigate the stability of a single and multi-soliton solution, which is found to be stable according to the spectral method. However, the stability is shown to be conditional, based on the energy method, and it depends on the dipole-dipole interaction strength. We find that the stability of the single-soliton solution is stable for certain interaction strengths, while it becomes unstable for others. We also observe that the stability of the multi-soliton solution is influenced by the dipole-dipole interaction strength, which is found to be stable for low interaction strengths and unstable for high interaction strengths. We provide numerical simulations to support our findings.

This paper explores a variety of mixed-integer optimization methods, including signomial and geometric programming variants, for solving complex problems involving non-linear relationships between variables. A key focus is on developing efficient methods for solving problems that involve both linear and non-linear constraints, as well as those that involve only non-linear constraints. The paper presents a novel approach to solving such problems, which leverages the properties of geometric programming to obtain optimal solutions. The method is based on a series of linear programming subproblems, which are solved using standard optimization techniques. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a variety of real-world problems, including portfolio optimization and machine learning. The results show that this approach can significantly improve the performance of existing methods, particularly for problems that involve both linear and non-linear constraints.

We propose novel approaches to the global Torelli conjecture for Teichmüller geodesics. The underlying idea draws from the relationship between the Teichmüller geodesic flow and the dynamics within Teichmüller spaces. Our theoretical framework is further substantiated by examples from the fields of global analysis and ergodic theory.

We introduce a novel method for creating a personalized, 3D model of an individual's appearance and shape using only a single video sequence. Our approach involves training a neural representation to predict an avatar's appearance from camera views, while also optimizing the model's pose and shape. This is achieved through a unique combination of a learned representation and a novel optimization technique that uses a 3D model to guide the optimization process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through a series of experiments, which show that it can generate high-quality avatars that accurately capture an individual's appearance and shape, even when viewed from previously unseen angles.

Recovering facial details from partially obscured images is a complex task, especially when the obstruction is made of objects like hands. To overcome this challenge, we suggest a novel method that combines a 3D facial model with a multi-stage deep learning approach. Our method first uses a 3D model to fill in obscured areas of the face, then refines the result with a network that learns from both the model and the image. This approach effectively blends the strengths of both techniques, producing high-quality facial reconstructions. Our method outperforms existing methods in terms of visual quality and accuracy, as shown by our experiments.

Intrinsic motivation is a concept that has been extensively researched in the field of reinforcement learning, with numerous applications in various domains. This study provides an overview of intrinsically-driven reinforcement learning, covering key aspects such as the definition and categorization of intrinsic motivation, learning methods, and relevant applications.

This study introduces a localized strategy iteration method for resolving team games in networked reinforcement learning. It is proven that this technique can efficiently solve any networked Markov team game. The key to this method lies in dividing the network into separate subgames based on the network's structure, allowing each agent to optimize its policy within its own subgame. The method is further enhanced by incorporating a neighborhood-based update rule that enables the agent to revise its policy when a neighboring agent updates its policy. The convergence of this method is supported by a rigorous proof, and its efficiency is demonstrated through various numerical experiments.

The results of a study on dijet events in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV are presented. Data were collected using the CMS detector at the LHC, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 1.55 inverse picobarns. The study focuses on events characterized by a notable rapidity gap between the leading and subleading jets. The rapidity gap is defined as the difference in rapidity between the leading jet and the nearest other jet. The analysis examines the rapidity gap distribution for leading jet rapidity values ranging from 0.3 to 2.4 and the leading jet transverse momentum between 150 and 1000 GeV/c. The study also investigates the leading jet's transverse momentum and rapidity distributions, as well as the rapidity gap distribution for leading jet transverse momentum values between 150 and 1000 GeV/c. The findings are compared with next-to-leading order perturbative QCD predictions and a next-to-next-to-leading order calculation.

Silicon, a widely used material in the electronics and photovoltaic sectors, has been known to have a low thermoelectric figure of merit. However, recent research has discovered that its two-dimensional form, silicene, exhibits improved thermoelectric properties. In this study, we have investigated the thermoelectric properties of penta-silicene, a two-dimensional silicene with a unique pentagonal structure. Our findings indicate that penta-silicene has a high thermoelectric figure of merit, which is significantly higher than that of bulk silicon and silicene. Furthermore, we have observed that penta-silicene has a high figure of merit at room temperature, which is comparable to the best known thermoelectric materials. Our research suggests that penta-silicene has the potential to be used in the development of efficient thermoelectric devices.

In this study, we investigate the impact of a strong magnetic field and temperature on the spectral properties of heavy quarkonia, specifically the bottomonium and charmonium families. Our analysis utilizes the fractional non-relativistic quark model, which we use to derive the quark-antiquark potential. We then apply this model to calculate the energy levels and decay widths of the quarkonia states in various magnetic field strengths and temperatures. Our results show that the magnetic field and temperature have significant effects on the energy levels and decay widths of the quarkonia states, which can be used to understand the behavior of these states in the quark-gluon plasma.

Dark matter particles that interact with each other can form compact clumps called subhalos, which may be present in abundance in the Milky Way. The study of dark matter scattering in these subhalos can provide valuable information about their internal structure. Researchers have proposed using various methods to investigate dark matter self-interactions, including neutron stars, cosmic rays, and ancient rocks. The neutron star method involves analyzing the mass and radius of the neutron star, while the cosmic ray method involves measuring the energy and direction of cosmic rays. The ancient rocks method involves analyzing the composition of the rocks. The study also examines the effects of different parameters on the scattering of dark matter particles and provides constraints on the properties of dark matter.

A significant class of signaling games, which includes models for detecting intrusions, monitoring processes, and scheduling inspections, is characterized by a trade-off between uncovering deception and maintaining optimal coverage. In these models, the sender's goal is to balance two competing objectives: encouraging the receiver to take action upon discovering a deceptive action and ensuring that the receiver checks all locations within a specified time frame. In this study, we examine a variation of the signaling game where the sender must adapt to an unknown environment, which can either be static or dynamic. In a static environment, the sender must determine a signaling strategy that maximizes the expected detection of deception while ensuring that all locations are monitored within a specified time frame. In a dynamic environment, the sender must adjust the signaling strategy in response to location changes, maintaining a balance between the expected detection of deception and the frequency of location changes. We develop a reinforcement learning algorithm that learns an optimal policy for the sender in both static and dynamic environments, and demonstrate that the algorithm achieves a suboptimal policy with a guaranteed error margin.

Robots capable of traversing uneven outdoor environments autonomously are highly sought after for their potential in search and rescue missions.  However, they must be able to adapt to rapidly changing environments and navigate around obstacles, all while maintaining stability.  To address these challenges, we've developed a novel framework, called TERP, that integrates two key components: a deep reinforcement learning-based planner and a robust control system.  The planner generates a reliable, long-term plan for the robot to follow, while the control system ensures the robot's movements remain stable and consistent.  By combining these components, we've created a framework that enables robots to navigate complex environments with greater efficiency and reliability.  We've tested our framework's performance in simulated environments and found that it outperforms existing methods in terms of both stability and speed.

We examine a two-dimensional inverse issue involving a planar inclusion with uniform conductivity, leveraging a recently developed regularisation technique for near-field data. This approach enables the construction of a regularisation function that is both differentiable and monotonic, ultimately facilitating novel iterative methods for solving the inverse inclusion problem.

The axially symmetric magnetic field is a widely used model in astrophysics, particularly in modeling the magnetic forces exerted by stars. Research has shown that this type of magnetic field is stable in a star's convective core, but its stability in a star's radiative core remains uncertain. To address this, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the stability of axially symmetric magnetic forces in stars, particularly in their radiative cores. Our investigation revealed that axially symmetric magnetic forces in a star's radiative core are generally stable, except for a specific scenario where the magnetic field is perpendicular to the radial direction. This finding has significant implications for understanding the magnetic forces exerted by stars and their potential impact on star's evolution.

This research paper explores the concept of simplicial coordination, a method for identifying and analyzing simplicial complexes through the lens of coordinate geometry, and its application in determining the topological properties of such complexes. By developing a framework for translating between complex structures and coordinate systems, we demonstrate the simplicial coordination's ability to facilitate seamless conversion and analysis. Furthermore, we examine the simplicial coordination's potential in uncovering hidden geometric and topological patterns within complex data sets, and we discuss its practical applications in fields such as data analysis and machine learning.

Linear algebra operations, particularly sparse matrix-vector multiplication and iterative linear solvers, are crucial components of various computational fields, including scientific computing and machine learning. The performance of these operations is significantly influenced by the sparsity pattern of the matrix, which can lead to memory access patterns that are difficult to optimize. This paper presents an in-depth analysis of the performance of iterative linear solvers, particularly the conjugate gradient method, on sparse matrices, and explores the impact of different matrix properties on their performance. The study also investigates the effectiveness of various optimization techniques, such as memory access optimization and algorithmic improvements, in improving the performance of these operations on sparse matrices.

We consider an entire function f(z) and an entire function of a specific form g(z), defined as the ratio of two entire functions, and demonstrate that f(z) and g(z) share a certain value IM for a certain uniqueness result to hold. This result has implications for the classification of g(z) in the context of Nevanlinna theory. Furthermore, we generalize a known theorem to the case of meromorphic functions of a certain order, sharing multiple finite values, and establish a common value shared by a collection of meromorphic functions of a certain order.

The widespread use of AR technology in everyday life is expected to increase, with wearable AR devices being a key component. However, users of these devices often struggle to understand the context of their surroundings, which can hinder their ability to effectively utilize AR technology. To address this challenge, we introduce the HAIR system, which utilizes computer vision and machine learning to automatically identify the purpose of objects in a wearer's environment. By combining HAIR with a wearable AR device, users can receive customized information about objects in real-time, enhancing their ability to navigate unfamiliar situations. Our research presents a comprehensive evaluation of HAIR's performance, including its ability to recognize objects in various contexts and its effectiveness in real-world applications.

The research establishes a key relationship between the integrability conditions of these systems and their associated Prolonged Lagrangian system. The study also demonstrates that any integrable system of this type corresponds to a specific type of connection, which can be used to derive the Monge-Ampère equation. The research further explores the properties of contact equivalence and shows that the Monge-Ampère system is invariant under this transformation. The study also introduces a new class of systems called Monge-Ampère systems with a pair of Lagrangian functions, which includes the generalized Monge-Ampère equation as a special case.
